newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN asks donors to pay $260 mln for Zaire relief.
newsitem.headline: UN asks donors to pay $260 mln for Zaire relief.

text.p: The United Nations urgently appealed to donors on Monday to provide $260 million to fund relief for hundreds of thousands of refugees in eastern Zaire.
The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA), releasing the flash appeal by U.N. agencies, said it would respond to the most urgent needs of refugees, returnees and the war displaced.

"The international community is faced with one of the largest humanitarian crises and is called upon to respond generously and without delay to this appeal," the DHA said in a statement at the U.N.'s European headquarters in Geneva.
The sudden flood of 500,000 Rwandan Hutus to Africa's most crowded country has caught aid agencies off-guard and will put new pressures on Western donors to assist them in home communes.
Until last week, the focus of relief efforts was on securing humanitarian corridors in eastern Zaire. Now agencies are scrambling to cope with an unprecedented number of returnees.

Ahead of the launch of the emergency appeal, U.N. officials in Geneva worked throughout the weekend revising budgets. Few could say where the remaining 500,000 refugees scattered in the region would be in a few weeks' time.
A million Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 after a rebel Tutsi army overran the country following the Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis.
In east Zaire, they set up up cinemas, brothels, shops and hotels in teeming tent cities where birth rates were among the world's highest.
In some camps, repatriation rates were so low that at times, the handful of returnees were being driven to the Rwandan border in air-conditioned, chauffeur-driven U.N. cars instead of buses.
In Rwanda, UNHCR said it was prepared for 10,000 returnees per day and was forced to review its operational requirements.
"The current crisis in eastern Zaire is unprecedented in the history of UNHCR," the refugee agency said in the appeal.

In Rwanda, housing will emerge as a key problem since many homes belonging to the refugees have been occupied by diaspora Tutsis -- 800,000 of whom returned home, almost a one-to-one replacement of the genocide dead, after Tutsis swept to power.
The refugees will need tools and seeds to get back into the agricultural cycle, as well as Western monitoring in villages where many will be accused of taking part in the genocide.

Diplomats also expect a surge in arrests and say lack of prison space will be one problem confronting the donors. Some 90,000 Hutus accused of genocide are jammed into overcrowded Rwandan jails, up from 18,000 early in 1995, and the starts of trials have been repeatedly delayed.
